INTERVIEW WITH CHAUNCEY MOREHOUSE BY ED HUTTO
We have a picture of you and your sister. What is her...?
Louise.
And she's still living in Philadelphia.
She married a rich doctor fellow.
I've been in contact with a historian down in Ocean City where you played with Art and Ted Weems.
That's right.
And we're trying to say are there any pictures around of where you may have played and he said, "well there were several free dance halls."
I have a couple of pictures of Art Weems.
Do you recall the name of the dance hall or wherever you might have played?
It was the Flanders Hotel, and one boardwalk cafe.
One boardwalk, maybe we can identify that.
Yes.
I notice in the pictures of the Specht band when it went to Europe....
Yeah.
There were lots apparently of wives.
That's right.
Were you married at the time or not?
No.
I noticed you were...either you were married and your wife took all the pictures.
She died.
I never saw Evelyn's or any with you.
Yes.
I saw some either with somebody named Dot or something. I don't know what it was. When did you marry?
It was '22 I think Al.
'22, that was 1921 then.
'22, that would make in 1923. And you were - the band went to Europe in the summer of '23. So it would be after that.
That's right, that's right.
In September.
Maybe in 1924 it was.
Now the Specht Band played in London in a room called the Corner Room or something to that effect.
The Corner House.
The Corner House.
Yeah.
Now you also went....
That was owned by a great, the biggest candy store in London. It was on the main street.
And I think you had a picture of that with an arrow pointing to that building.
Yes, that's right. The Lions.
And I have a reference in a book by Brian Rust in England about the band playing possibly.
Lion Corner House.
Now you went to France, Did you play in France or not?
No, I didn't.
It was just part of the vacation.
Yeah.
And you flew over from...
From London.
In the Hanley Page aircraft.
That's right.
We have pictures of that.
Because none of the Frenchmen knew us at all. And they didn't want to take a chance on putting a rough guy in there and spoiling their caliber of music.
Now in your album, there is a picture of a recording session I guess at Columbia. Now I know you made records for Columbia in England.
Yeah.
Perchance, was that picture taken in England or do you remember?
I would have to see the music.
Okay.
I would see the picture.
The picture is extended out, hung from the ceiling.
It had wires, you know.
Yes.
And then would come down a music stand. And on that music stand, we would put the music and just stand right up to play it, and bend it a little bit so that the music didn't go right into the stand.
So if you had a solo, you'd maybe go up to the horn.
Yes, that's right. And everybody had to memorize their own solo.
Was there any particular reason why you left the Specht Band?

Yes, Specht had lost his respect. And he got a hotel job which I didn't like, Alamac Hotel. Yeah. And I didn't like that job at all because there was too much to do, too much responsibility. He would leave the stand for two hours at a time and say, 'the band is in your charge,' like that. Now every so often he would put me in charge of the band and I didn't like that. And the tunes that I called out, the guys in the band didn't like. And I thought I was
picking out the very best things the Specht band played. But it wasn't.
But they did play them.
Yeah, yeah.
Now were you married at the time you left the Specht Band?
Yes, I was married at the time I joined it.
And you went back with Ted Weems for a while, in the midwest or just wherever...
Yeah, well I went with Ted Weems periodically. If he were in Pittsburgh and I was in Columbus, Ohio, he would tell me to come to Columbus and sit in, you know because he loved me.
And you were in that situation when Russ Morgan contacted you about going to the Goldkette Band?

Yes. Well we were two Pennsylvania guys. And Russ got me on the phone and he said, do you remember me, Russ Morgan? I come from the coal miner country up in Pennsylvania. I says sure, I remember you. I didn't.
The Weems band broke up...
That is the Weems band broke up.
The Weems band broke up because he couldn't pay the salary. He couldn't get enough of the... (Inaudible)... go to Detroit, I know.
Here's a little different question. I assume you're sort of an original drummer and all like that but did any other drummer have any influence on your style or what you did?

No, none of them. Because I was so strictly left-handed that I couldn't copy a right-handed drummer. I just couldn't copy him. And I often wished that there was a drummer that I could take lessons from. And one drummer did teach me how to make a better roll. You know my roll was ticka ticka ticka ticka ticka...tick, instead of Rrrrrrr, you know.
Now any other drummers in particular that you admire their work?

Well at the Alamac Hotel, we didn't have very many subs, unless some guy was sick. And there would be a sub come in and everybody didn't like him because he didn't like the band sound like it should have sounded, you know. So that's that story.
Well, during the twenties, did people like Baby Dodds or Zotty Singleton...
No, we didn't have much truck with the colored people.
You didn't. Uh huh.
If you want to hear the colored people, go up there Saturday night after we're through. And they played till 5 in the morning. I'd sit there and listen.
And I was listening to the best colored musicians in New York. So that's what we had to do.
Did you ever hear Chick Webb?
Yeah, yup.
Were you impressed? Well did you know Krupa early in his career?
No, I didn't know him too well. I heard of him and that he was the greatest drummer around. And I heard of him but he and I were never thrown together. Either they had me or they had him.
Virginia Morehouse: There was a writeup in the paper... And I was very impressed with it because it said Chauncy was the better musician and...

Well I had studied piano. I could play piano. And I studied other instruments as well. Now some of the clarinet players put me through well everything because that was the funniest name the musicians had ever heard - Chauncey.
I believe you said once before that a Catholic nun, maybe you took piano lessons from her.

Yes, I took piano lessons from the Catholic sisters. Now Sister Gabriel was my teacher. She was my teacher. And Sister whatever it was, there was a half a dozen out there that gave me piano lessons. But I took from Sister Gabriel. And she liked me very much. And she gave me
more knowledge on the piano than anyone else.
But the drums as such, you picked up on your own in the school bands and...

I tried out for the school band and the leader was a woman, Susanne Lenz her name was. And she says, he's it. And there were three or four other drummers playing in the band, you know. I'd play one tune. And they would play four more. And she picked me out because this guy is a natural.
Your father played on the piano.
Yeah, yeah.
Did he give you any lessons or did you copy anything from him?
No, he never gave me any lessons. He was too busy getting the right note himself. And he just played what he knew. And I knew exactly what he was going to play before he sat down to the piano.
Now say the vibraphone, did you play the xylophone or the vibraphone? Was it around at that time?
No, I didn't...I had a little xylophone about this long. And I used to pick out little easy things to play on that.
So you were self taught more or less on that.
Tick tick tick tick tock, ticka ticka ticka tock, you know. But I took up the vibraphone and the
xylophone when I went to NBC, to be the drummer at NBC. And that taught me a helluva lot. And I went to the best teacher in New York.
Well I guess we're about ready to jump to that period. After the Goldkette Band, you more or less went into - I guess you made a few records with Howard Lanin.
Yes.
And maybe Don Vorhees.
Don Vorhees, yes.
And the Hit of the Week, the paper record, the paid for records.
Yes, yeah.
And at that time about the late twenties, you got with NBC.
That's right.
Now who were the more or less useful directors there, Frank Black or Nat Schilkret or anybody like that?

Nat Schilkret was one of them. And although he didn't know jazz at all. He'd have to take our word for what's good jazz. So Nat Schilkret, I think was the - I worked for him more than anyone else. He liked me, on account of my easy going way, my pace. He liked my pace. So that was it.
Now did you make records with Victor Young and the Brunswick orchestra?
Yes, many.
Now were you on any of the early Bing Crosby projects?
Yeah.
How about the Face the Music medley where he sang 'Soft Lights and Sweet Music'. There is a vibraphone in that.
I don't remember that tune exactly. "Soft lights and sweet music....."
That's one of the rag theme records, yes.
Yeah.
There is a vibraphone on it and I just wondered if it might be you.
Well it might be. Because I had a terrific memory. And I'd hear a piece once and I could stand up at the vibraphone and not make a mistake.
I'll have to bring that record some time.
I wish you would.
That might show but you probably - easy to miss there. Now supposedly you were in some of the Boswell Sisters recordings.
Oh the Boswell Sisters were my friends.
Were you in "When I Take My Sugar to Tea". One just started, just says yes, one says Stan King. So you never know.
No, it wasn't Stan King.
And there was one, 'Concentrating on You', I think Connie alone, you're supposedly on that.
Yeah, I did most everything when the Boswell Sisters went with NBC. I did most all of their records unless I was sick or something like that.
Now they started with CBS. Did they switch to NBC some time later?
Yeah.
And then in '34, they were of course in Hollywood with Bing on Woodbury's shows. So I guess this was in '33 or so in New York probably.
I guess so, yes.
Okay. Now the drums that you invented, what do you call that?
Tune drums.
G-N-O-M, Gnama or what do you say?
G-N-O-M-A drums.
Ngoma.
Ngoma?
Like N-'-G-O-M-A.
Ngoma, now is that....
Yes and I got that out of a dictionary. And I went through all the drums in the dictionary to find out what the hell to call these things. And this was a
South American drum. And they used it a lot down in New Orleans and all of that stuff. And I thought that would be good for me. It sounds African, N'goma, N-G-O-M-A, N'goma.
Now did that imply a type of drums or a set of drums.

A type of drum. It was a drum this high and this big around with one head on it at the top. If you would put a head on the bottom, you wouldn't get any true tone. So you tune it with a key up here. And every day I would have to come in and tune the drum and scale-wise you know.
Now along about 1937, you had your audition band that we had. Now do you know about how much before that you invented the drums or came up with the set?
Well I don't know. It must have been, oh it must have been a good five years.
So you'd been working from 1932 or so, all during that period.
Yes. In fact, because I had the N'goma drums, this is why they wanted me as leader because it would be something different to present to the public.
Now you made this audition record in November of 1937 at NBC. Do you recall anybody who was in the band? It sounds real great but I don't recognize any of the soloists.
All of the best musicians are in the band, the ones who could fake and you know I can't
remember any of them now. But we had the cream of the crop of NBC.
Now you had that audition band. Did you have it in a hotel or did you really do anything with it?

No, this is strictly for the NBC programs. And they said Chauncey Morehouse and his N'goma band, you know. And that meant my turn was coming up. And then I would play two or three tunes and that would be it.
But you actually were on radio programs on NBC as your band.
Yes, yes.
Was it - any particular programs you recall or...?
No particular programs because this....
Was sort of sustaining.

This music, dance music went on anyhow. So if I hadn't have been there, it would have gone on. And they'd have had some other star do what he could do best, you know. So that was the story about that.
Well I brought some tape here with some records. And we'll play some after a while.
All right.
Some of the things from that era. We have the - maybe I shouldn't tell you what it was and let you guess at them - but there are some Chick Bulluck sides in there.
I think you made some records with Chick Bulluck.
Chick Bulluck.
Yes.
That name sound familiar.
Maybe you'll recognize at least one of them.
Was he a colored guy?
No, he wasn't I don't think, I don't think. But he made oodles of records in the thirties. Maybe you'll recognize some of them.
Yeah.
One of the records I have of yours is the Bluebird Military Band and this is in 1934 that it was recorded.
Yeah, that was an NBC name, the Bluebird Military Band.
Yes, the Bluebird was the 35¢ Victor label.
Most of the time we did marches and stuff like that, you know. In the military band, you play military style, they told me.
Now you made - I was with Irving Mills who had Master Records was the name of it. That was it and then Variety was their 35¢ label.
Well I write with Irving Mills.
Oh you did. Under what circumstances?
He printed everything that I wrote.
He was the publishing house and I guess he managed the Ellington band among others.
That's right. And he was in the Roseland building upon on Broadway. So everything that I'd write, I'd take right down to Irving Mills.
So that's sort of how you got into making the records for him, the Master Records.
Yeah, that's right, that's right.
I found them. I've got copies of them for you.
You have?
The "My Gal Sal," "On the Alamo," "Blues in B Flat," "Plastered in Paris".
"Plastered in Paris", "that's my tune".
Yes. I think...
"Blues in B Flat" is my tune.
They list Mills as the composer of "Plastered in Paris" but did you compose it or not? I think it says Mills and Marks.
Well Mills put his name on everything.
I think he did that in a lot of the Ellington things that had Ellington and Mills.
That's right. Mills put his own name on everything that he sold.
Well we have that and we'll play them for you after a while.
All right, I wish you would.
Okay, there is one more there. On one side of the record it's Johnny Williams.
Johnny Williams.
Is he a drummer?
He was my rival.
That side, you know he really beats it out.
Yeah, oh he was a hell of a good drummer. I wish I had his facility.
He plays 'I'll Build a Stairway to Paradise.' And it was the song that Charlie Spivak, some of the same people that were on the other side.
That's right, that's right.
Now let's see, when you were with Leith Stevens on the Saturday Night Swing Club, were you still associated with NBC or not?
No, that was after
After.

Because when I got into radio, I talked to a big shot in the radio and he says 'now look, you can't be wandering around here doing work for everybody. You belong as of this moment to us. And we will tell you what to do. We'll keep you working. But you'll play what we tell you to play.'
Well I guess the Fred Allen show was essentially on NBC....
The Fred Allen show, yeah, yeah.
But you were on it, I believe you said for 7 years or 5 years.
Yeah.
But then when you were in the Saturday Night Swing Club on CBS, you still did the NBC Fred Allen? Peter Van Steeden?
Peter Van Steeden, yes. Because I went with Pete's band and stayed there until he broke up.
How late is that? I don't recall. How long was it?
The Peter Van Steeden thing?
Yes, did that run up to World War II or not?
Oh yes, that was quite long.
So you were associated with them.
Yes.
On the Saturday Night Swing Club, was that program off for several years? I remember it but not definitely.
Saturday Night Swing Club.
Did it have guests?
No; that was always on Saturday night.
But most every night we had a guest like Bunny Berigan And it just changed our style for that tune alone. And then everybody would applaud him. He was great, just absolutely great.
Now the Leith Stevens Band made four sides for Vocalion. Were you on that?
Leith Stevens?
And the Saturday Night Swing Club, the orchestra made four records.
It it was the Saturday Night Swing Club, I was on it.

'Love's Old Sweet Song', we brought those. We'll play those for you, 'Twelfth Street Rag.' And the 'Royal Garden Blues' which is really the 'Memphis Blues'. Okay, we'll play those for you. When Larry Clinton started his band, I guess it was just a recording band at first and apparently you were on the second recording session he had.
Well Larry Clinton came into the NBC because his records were selling. And NBC wanted a guy whose records Could sell. So that's why they got him.
To sort of tie in with RCA and NBC.
Yeah, yeah.
So you were on both sides of that.
There were only a couple of big record makers, Columbia, RCA.
Okay now, when the war time came in the forties, were you still predominantly in radio? And I know these jingles on the floating tin cans or something....
Yeah, yeah.
Well you were still a staff musician at NBC then or...?

You know I'd have to look that up. I really couldn't tell you. But I was with NBC for a hell of a long time. And I don't really remember now because life was going by and I just couldn't remember everything I was connected with.
Were you ever on the Telephone Hour or the Firestone program?
Both.
You were on both.
I played the Telephone Hour for Don Voorhees.
You did. And the Voice of Firestone.
And the Voice of Firestone, I played maybe a haf a dozen programs.
Okay, I have a transcriptions of one of those here and we'll work that in too.
Yeah.
On Hobby Lobby, we have the script. In there you played 'Flat Foot Floogie' on the drums.
Yeah, that was my tune. "The Flat Foot Floogie with the floy floy, dee dee dee do da dee, do do da da do da da. Floy doy, floy doy, floy doy."
Are the drums up in your attic?
Yeah.
How big a deal is it to bring them down? Are they all dusty or what?
Well the biggest drum is like this.
I mean some time. What I'd like to do some time is to, if you can, play "Flat Foot Floogie", if we could tune them. And I'll record that little, sort of work it in.
Yeah, I could play that.

Let's see there's a lot of music we can put in here but not too many pictures. That is we don't have that many pictures to go through. So what I'd like to do is just to have pictures of the drums, you know close up, one drum at a time.
Yes.

All sorts of things like that, just to get...Could we set them up in that room some time? Is it big enough or not? Okay, we'll do that some time at your convenience. Now did you make any records with the Sauter-Finnegan band?
No.
We have some Sauter-Finnegan records here and I didn't know whether you did or not.
Well they were given to me to study.
Okay.

So that I could get the idea. Because a lot of recording musicians said if you could play this, I'll hire you. And if you can play that and this and this and that, you know. They had their own style and they didn't want to break into it.
I assume Russ Case was a friend of yours.
Yeah.
You seem to have been with him with Russ Morgan and then you made that one LP that I have of yours which you played. The Carey Dancers, I can hear your drums on that.
(HUMS A FEW BARS OF THE CAREY DANCERS)
Did you ever make...I don't know whether... Did Case ever accompany Perry Como on recordings? Maybe it's Mitch Ayres, I'm not too sure.
I think it was Mitch Ayres. I don't think Russ Case ever did that. He was sort of a stay-to-myself guy.
But he was a good trumpet man.
Yeah, yeah.
What surprised me on those sides is your Varsity sides with Spivak. Generally you don't hear Spivak like that.
Oh no. His was what was called fast musicians in that day. And he gave a little more.
And I guess he was with Bob Crosby right after that.
Yeah.

Now let's see where are we. Oh as the radio sort of died down in the fifties and television came in, you were of course with the City Service Band and Paul Lavalle. What else were you doing in the sixties? Were you...
I was making records mostly.
Just wherever the opportunity occurred.
Yeah, Columbia Records, down at the Victor or - that was my extra-curricular work, making records, for the people who liked my records.
Well seeming the sort of Latin American music was coming in at that time.
That's right. I had no problem with Latin American music.
I know. You do 'Jamaica Farewell'.
Because it's all drumming, you know.
Well this one, you have something called 'Swamp Buggy'. Is that...
'Swamp Buggy.'
Was that something you composed?
That was mine.
And there is a whole band backing you on that.
That's right.
What was the situation?
Now I forget how 'Swamp Buggy' went. Is it recorded?
Yeah I wondered why it was made, who it was with. And you do 'Avalon' on one other.
What is it on the tapes?
Well some of it is on the tape and some of it is on those big records. So I don't know what...
I did 'Swamp Buggy'. Yeah.
I think it says the first 'Swamp Buggy' or something.
(HUMS A FEW BARS OF THE MELODY)
Now let's see. Getting back to the pictures in that book. There was a loose picture of a little baby in a crib. Now what is the - about when did that come along?
Well my son was born, you know.
The first?
Yeah, he was the oldest.
His first son was born. He died.
Do you know who he is? Jack, he died.
He was born in '26. There is a picture of a boy by a car in New York. Now is that Jack?
That's Jack.
And how old was he then?
He was about four. He up and died.
The picture looks a little old. So he died about 1933?
Yeah.
And now did you have a daughter?
Yes, Susan.
Susan. And another son.
No, just a boy and a girl. That's all we had.
Then Jimmy was born in 1930 something.
Yeah, 1933, something like that. Now isn't it funny that I forget when they were born.
So there were two sons and one died and a daughter. And a son and daughter still?
Yeah. And we were a very unhappy family.
Due to the fact that the child died.
Yeah.
That was very hard to take.

But we came out of it fine. Well I came out of it fine because where I worked, they always gave me encouragement. There is no else except you and you're the only one that knows how to play these drums and by God, you get out there and do your best.
There is in some of the material you had, after the Shell Company called the Bandstand.
That's beautiful.
Well generally in say this period of the sixties, in addition to making records whatever at the time, did you have any other business activities?
Yes, I was called constantly from other orchestra leaders to make records, at Columbia.
... the Goldman Band.
The Goldman Band, I was a steady.
Well they played, was that a year round type of activity or mostly in the summer in New York.
Well that was more year around, they played nothing but marches, you know, the Goldman Band. And I was playing in the Chambersburg Band, snare drum at the same time. So I knew how to play....
Of all the bands you played with, which was the most fun or the most rewarding?
I think the Paul Specht band.
Even more than the Goldkette band?
Yes because he gave me more liberty than anybody else.
I guess it lasted a few years.
And we played at the Alamac Hotel.
On Bix's last recording session with Hoagy Carmichael, some of them say you're in it. Some say you aren't. "A Night in Havana", "Betsy Didn't Help It."

Bix didn't use me as much as he could have. And he would have a record date and I would have a record date. And there was no way of keeping track of Bix. And I wasn't a good enough businessman to see that I kept track with him. Because I was a big shot. And I was up here a big shot. And I thought what the hell, if they want me, they'll call me.
But do you recall..making...okay, there is one thing I didn't bring tonight. Apparently you were in again an Irving Mills Hopsy Topsy Gang, 1929.
Yeah.
With Carmichael and one of the things you played was 'Stardust'. This was before they had lyrics to it.
Yeah, that's right. I did that.
And 'March of the Hoodlums'.
"March of the Hoodlums", yeah.
I didn't bring that this time but I will bring it for you.
That would be very precious to me.
Yeah, okay. On the recording of 'On the Alamo', we can hear you playing vibes. We hear something, people are hand clapping, you couldn't play the vibes and the drums at the same time.
No, no. ( HUMS A FEW BARS)

We'll play that in a little bit. Now let me see. I think I have a couple more questions on here. Gee, I think I've about asked everything here. Of all the musicians you've played with, any of them strike you as being the best?
The epitome.
Yes. Which in particular did you most admire?
Well I liked Fuzzy Farrar, the trumpet player. He was top trumpet, five miles away from my home, at an orphanage. And he led the band down there. He played the lead and led the band and was loud.
Was this in Pennsylvania?
Yeah. Scotland School. Scotland was five miles south of Chambersburg towards Schippensburg.
He thought that Specht was his favorite.
You thought that Specht was the band and a little more freedom.
Yeah Specht was my favorite. As far as my career was concerned, I'd rather play for Specht.
because he let me have my own head. And nobody else would.
(Inaudible comment about Goldkette band)
The Gold Cat band yes, but that was years and years later.
You were a jazz nut.
Yeah, that's right.
I don't know. We'll discuss how personal we want to make some of these things. And when did Evelyn...?
Evelyn, I met her at a dance at the Alamac Hotel.
So you met her in New York.
That's where we were playing with Paul Speck. And she was a gorgeous looking woman.
Was she in show business or not?
No. Everybody said she should be. But she was a gorgeous girl.
A number of the pictures you have, I guess I recognized. Her hair was up.
Yeah.
(inaudible comment)
Well don't go to lunch and we can do this later. And how long did she last?
Who's that?
Evelyn did.
Yeah, about that. About 64 yeah.
(Inaudible comment)
Now was he still in New York at the time?
Yes.
Now did I understand correctly that some time after that you...
I wrote a book on that.
I would like him to do that.
Oh I see.
Are you trying to establish how we met one another.
I think he said you met at one of the Goldkette reunions with Bix.

It was Don Ho, Don Ho that's right. And they had called all the Goldkette men. And Doc and Norma (RYKER) with whom I had kept correspondence with. Doc over night and we were going through this big thing and I had.. And it was called.. Chicago. But he was delighted. So he went up there all but I could hardly tell them.. It was like 50 years since I set eyes on them. But I said who compares them, Detroit, at the Gold Cat band and they all turned around and still shocked. I knew that this was too much. We were pretty.
Now this place you were mentioning, is that in Jersey or was this...?
Jersey, uh huh. 150 miles.
Yeah the memorial was in Jersey but all of the Detroit boys were there.
John Donna, Bill Donna Ho had this every year.
What year was this.
Nineteen thirty something.
(Inaudible comment)
This was your sister.
Yes.
And what's her last name?
Siebert, Hazel Siebert.....
And I found a gal I loved.
Good.
He wrote a beautiful song about it.
So looking at the various songs that Chauncey has written, are they...You can't accuse him of writing romantic ballads that maybe he could... Ed Brown and Incline Rise...
A man with a — named Brown was the meanest individual in this town. He would burn every time the tune was mentioned. In other words, bring to his

attention. Let the big old bump made him look like a clown. There was a bumpfy there named Brown. And you know what we called him, bump on the head Brown. Bump on the head Brown, he was the meanest man in town.
(inaudible comment)
strategy... jazz band. But this was a ballad...
I guess for Bix, what is it, 'Ringing and Twisting,' he wrote that supposedly.
No.
No, I think he probably gave you credit.
I think so. 'Ringing and Twisting', I don't remember that.
You don't remember that.
No.

Okay and I mentioned on the phone that I had contacted this man who has old records, that I've gotten records from him. And I went over there Saturday. And he has a number of Paul Specht records and a number of the Georgian records.
Oh yes.
And they are $3 a piece. So I thought maybe we could decide on if you wanted to get any or I want a few of them of course. And he said drop him a note and he will pick them out.
Well they were rather old-fashioned style.
Well let's call out some. If any of them strike your fancy, we'll make sure we get them. Now one of them, let's see...Apparently before you made records for Columbia, you made one for Paramount.
Paramount, yeah.
He has that.

The headline is "African Rhythm in Drum Device." It is a far cry from the primitive blatant beating of African tom toms to the raucous swinging tempos of our present day jazz tribes in cafes and ballrooms. Yet by an ingenius device invented by Chauncey Morehouse, orchestra leader, authentic African rhythms, the basic foundation of all swing music has been injected into American jazz. Morehouse has contributed the newest innovation in the music world, the N'goma drums. It is an instrument of his own design which consists of routine snare drums of varying sizes which are tuned chromatically, making it possible for the first time in musical history to play melody as well as rhythm on a percussion instrument. "The three year labor put into the construction of this instrument," explains Morehouse, "was inspired by the necessity to relieve swing music of the monotonous four-four tempo. By adding a melodic tone to its rhythm, the tempo can become musical. Many thought the instrument would be impractical but I think our recent phonograph recording proved it to be an advantageous feature to swing music." Morehouse first conceived the idea while making a survey of African music for the NBC Music

Library. In the Belgian Congo, he learned that a tribe known for its elaborate drum music, the natives used no melody instruments but contrived their music from intricate drum sets. In a New York public library, he also discovered music manuscripts of original African chants and adapted this native music to modern jazz interpretation. "Swing music for the main part," said Morehouse, "is improvised notes because the Africans had no way of writing their music, it was handed down from father to son and each generation sang and played its own interpretation of the melodies. In our music, this is known as ad libbing and is the most important phase of jazz occurring in every orchestra performance. The flexibility of the African songs made them suitable to jazz compositions such as 'Mazi-Pani*' and 'Ku-li-a' which we recently recorded." These two compositions were created by Morehouse. Mazi-Pani is a working song, comparable to early American railroad ditties and translated freely means, I do not like a man who is lying down. Ku-li-a is a hunting song sung in celebration of a big kill and means here is food to eat. When questioned further about the construction of N'goma, of his N'goma drums, Morehouse explained that his big problem in designing them was obtaining skins or drum heads the thickness of which would be in proportion to the size of the particular drum. It was the continuous switching of skins selected from various animals in a search to find the one with the best tone that created the most serious barricade to

ultimate success. After three years of patient experimenting, Morehouse was able to present his N'goma drums to the music world and public at large. Aside from the fact that N'goma drums are an important innovation to jazz music, they have immense possibilities in symphonic music, according to Irving Mills, music impressario and Morehouse's manager. "Forest Hills drummer with a boogie beat has played the happy music for 30 years. If the residents of Forest Hills' Ingram Street suddenly hear a Dixieland drumbeat, the sound of a vibraharp, kettledrums or any other percussion instrument, they won't wonder where it's coming from. Chauncey Morehouse, a jazz drummer with almost 30 years of the happy music behind him lives at 68-31. Happy music, that's right, said the 48 year-old jazz man who plays all percussion instruments as well as piano and banjo. That's how I felt when I first heard Dixieland 30 years ago. It made me smile. I felt happy. Morehouse, who has been living on Ingram Street for 15 years, was born in Niagara Falls, N.Y.

He started playing in his high school band in Chambersburg, Pennsylvania. He got his first paid job playing a banjo for Ted Weems in the early twenties. "Ted and I were kids together" Morehouse said, "and he offered me this spot playing banjo. I took it and I was in business". From the Weems band, Morehouse went to various other dance units in the 1920s. Among them, the orchestras of Paul Whiteman, Jean Goldkette and Red Nichols and His Five Pennies. He's played on the same stand with most of the jazz musicians who made the music in the twenties and are still playing in Greenwich Village niteries. Radio was in its infancy then. And the main source of dance music for the home was the phonograph. Morehouse made countless sides with four or five man pickup bands including other young musicians of the day such as Artie Shaw, Russ Morgan, Jimmy and Tommy Dorsey, Benny Goodman, Glenn Miller and a current player called Leon "Bix" Beiderbecke Beiderbecke who was a close friend of the Forest Hills drummer, was known as the owner of the hottest horn in jazz until he died of pneumonia, 30 years old in 1931. He was also the model for Dorothy Baker's Young Man With a Horn. Nobody could live that kind of life and reach old age, Morehouse said. "Like a lot of kids today who suddenly discover they can play great jazz, Bix forgot everything else, lived too fast, drank a steady diet of gin and orange juice and never bothered about his health. He played his heart out. And it just gave up on him

all of a sudden." Morehouse met his wife, Evelyn, in 1924 when he was supposed to be preparing to enter the Boston Conservatory of Music, his father's idea. "I was supposed to enter in September," Morehouse said. "I had my choice, marry Evelyn and play jazz music or put it off, study theory and harmony. And we got married in August. That settled it."

The Morehouses have two children, James 19 and Suzanne 15. "When Jimmy came along, I knew I'd have to settle down," Morehouse said. "I'd been in radio since 1928 and I hadn't made up my mind to stay. That clinched it." He's been in radio orchestras ever since. At present he plays in the studio orchestras of the NBC programs, the City Service Band, Break the Bank and the Sunday Longine Hour. In his spare time, Morehouse goes fishing on Great South Bay. He's the proud owner of a 25 foot cruiser, the Sueve II, part of the fleet of the South Shore Power Squadron. "The greatest contribution to American music in the 20th century," Morehouse says, "is Dixieland jazz." "And don't believe it's old hat or losing popularity," he said. "The proof of that is in the youngsters have a record collection that will go through the floor if they get any more. They think it's something new and fascinating. And jazz started something like 50 years ago."
As for the newest fad in popular music, bebop, Morehouse hasn't a great deal of love for it. "There are always fads in the arts," he said, "and in our music bop is the latest.

They say you've got to understand it. Who wants to understand a lot of honking that goes disguised as music. Bop musicians talk about the flatted fifth,"he said, "That kind of discord is fine if you played in a symphony orchestra and spread the notes out among the instruments so that you can get beautiful color tones. But when four or six pieces try, it's nothing more than a discordant noise. Give me the old Dixie two beat," he said. "Playing in a Dixieland outfit is like being part of a huge throbbing machine. You become part of the music. You sit down with a bunch of right guys to play Dixie and it comes out strong and happy. That's it. That's the end."

This one is entitled "Chauncey Morehouse of Forest Hills collects Weird Drums". The subtitle is - has 14 tuned to different pitches upon which tunes can be played. And the article reads: Remember those travelogues you saw in the movies where wild savages played weird tomtoms. You saw the savages but the drums you heard were probably played in a Manhattan studio by Chauncey Morehouse of 68-41 Ingram Street, Forest Hills. Morehouse, who has played the drums for all kinds of music, has gathered a collection of exotic drums from all parts of the world. "I didn't start out to be a collector," Morehouse explained. "It was simply that I asked friends of mine who were traveling to bring back drums from various countries for me. Then at the radio studios, it was found that certain drums gave grand sound effects for drama as well as music. Now most of my drums are at sound effects studios because the sound engineers have borrowed them." Morehouse has 14 drums mounted on a semi-circular bar, each tuned to a different pitch. Tunes can be played on the drums which range through the scale from B flat to B flat, leaving one extra drum which may be tuned to any low pitch. They are known as the N'goma drums. Morehouse designed them and borrowed the name from the N'goma drum of South Africa. Actually there is no resemblance. The African

N'goma is a single drum shaped like a giant egg cup, large at the top and small at the bottom with skins on each end. The Africans dance right on the drum at tribal jam sessions, beating out the rhythm as they dance. Morehouse's drums open up a new field to the musician. The instruments do not replace ordinary ones or the tympany but represent a new musical instrument. By using different types of sticks, Morehouse achieves different effects from Boleros and Rhumbas to oriental tones. Morehouse is enthusiastic about the drums because they are melody instruments and give the player freedom for improvisation. He has played them in a film short in which he was featured with Leith Stevens and the Swing Club Orchestra. A drummer with Major Bowes on the Sunday Morning Capitol Theater Family, Morehouse has played drum specialties several times including one on his N'goma drums. Six years ago Morehouse played for a full length moving picture in which difficult sounds like the trumpeting of elephants had to be dubbed in. He found himself a sound effects man achieving all kinds of sounds including pistol shots with his drums. Morehouse was complimented for his expert rhythm. His only guide was the hands of the natives appearing in the picture. He provided the drum music for a whole series of travelogues. Recordings of Morehouse and his N'goma drums in original compositions have been made. They include "Mazi-panf and "Ku-li-ay." Although Morehouse denies he is an expert on ancient and

foreign drums, he is rapidly becoming one. He admits that although it didn't start as a hobby, his collection is proving so engrossing, it is rapidly becoming one. Piece by piece, he has collected an unusual set of drums from foreign countries. One of them is a clay drum shaped like a vase from Turkey. When he uses it in radio work, he can make it double for an African drum. "In Turkey," Morehouse explained, "the drum is really a duet instrument and is played with a three string mandolin. The mandolin, a long necked instrument, has loose strings which are twanged. The drum is played with the hands and is often heard in hashish houses". Another strange piece which Morehouse insists is classified as a percussion instrument is the jawbone of an ass, painted pink with silver teeth. The sound is achieved by shaking. And the rattling of the teeth produces the sound. The jawbones are used for rhumbas. Morehouse says it is a percussion instrument because a blow is used to make the sound. Two white small drums, mounted on the same stick come from Cuba. They are usually played with the hand on one and a stick on the other. Again, different sounds can be achieved by using different types of sticks. Often they are played with dried gourds. His South African drums are covered with goatskins, even with goat fur. Others are covered with calfskin and pigskin. Morehouse explained the drums vary in Africa as much as do the spoken dialects. There is no set pattern for drums.

A large Chinese tomtom, double headed is being used in a radio studio. 18 inches wide and deep, the sides are made to bulge out in order to stand the strain of the terrific tension of the pigskin covering. The drum is used to attract attention to Chinese theaters, Morehouse explained. He also has two Chinese hand drums mounted on sticks. They are filled with pebble-like pieces and operate like a rattle. The sound is achieved by turning the hand. These instruments are used in festivals and parades. A weirdly pink drum from Haiti is another in Morehouse's collection. A strange one from Indo-China is one of his favorites. Four feet long, the drum doesn't resemble any others. Sound is produced by rubbing a hand over it as with a tambourine. Morehouse explained the drum is used for sending signals because the sound carries only in the direction that the instrument is pointed. The sound. The sound thus travels to its destination without being heard by neighboring villages not in the track of its sound. Morehouse has an engagement to make 12 recordings in which his drum music is featured. Only a few of the drums are in Morehouse's home at 68-41 Ingram Street. The others remain in their radio studios. In spite of Morehouse's growing fame as a drum collector, he is "strictly a dance band man." His own words. He started playing the drums when he was 12. He was born in Niagara Falls but his family moved to Chambersburg, Pennsylvania when he was an infant. He

studied piano but started to play the drums without lessons until he found out that there were better drummers than he. Then he studied. When he was in high school, he played with the school band and joined the summer band from Gettysburg College. The band played in Ocean City, New Jersey. When that broke up, Morehouse got a job with a dance orchestra playing the banjo and was good enough to get by. Soon he persuaded the manager to let him send for his drums. Musicians in those days were versatile fellows. Morehouse used to alternate between the drums, the xylophone and a few other instruments. He organized the Versatile Five in which the trumpet player also played the violin and the pianist played the ocharina. When he finished school, he took a job in Pittsburgh with the Harrison-Hollins orchestra. Next he helped Paul Specht form a band which went on a successful trip to England in 1923. He finished his three-year contract with Speck and went with Ted Weems. When the band was reorganized, he joined the Jean Goldkette band. Morehouse's cymbal playing became a byword. When the Goldkette band broke up in 1927, Morehouse went with Don Vorhees's orchestra. It was in 1928 that he started to work on radio. All along, he had been doing recordings. In those days, Morehouse explained, the big band leaders didn't have regular bands. When they got record dates, they called the musicians they wanted. Morehouse was so much in demand, he was kept busy working on records alone.

Name almost any famous band and you will find Morehouse was the drummer on its most popular recordings. After 1928, he stayed on the radio except for brief intervals with Rubinoff and Roger Wolf Kahn. He gave up playing the drums in musical comedies ten years ago. Morehouse says it's a lazy man's job. You learn a score and then play it the same way night after night with your eyes shut, he commented. He played for Rain or Shine and Follow Thru. Morehouse has had to play opera and concert for the radio but his true love is swing. He was the suitcase man with such swing cats as the late Bix Beiderbecke, Miff Moll and Frank Trumbauer. He wrote "Crazy Cat" and "Three Blind Mice" in collaboration with Trumbauer.

Mrs. Morehouse is amused at the $1.98 royalty checks that still come in for those songs which were written 12 years ago. Saxophone solos arranged for the music by Trumbauer are used by most sax students today. Morehouse wrote other songs and confesses the musicians in those days who had record dates would make recordings of their own music and then try the publisher which was much easier than trying to find a publisher first. He hopes to organize a band of his own soon. First, he must reorganize his household. The family is in the throes of moving. Even though it's only down the block. After April 1, the Morehouse address will be 68-31 Ingram Street. He has two children, Suzanne-4 and Jimmy-7. The family moved to Forest Hills from Rego Park five years ago.
